Do I believe that the 2020 election was swung by errors?
No.

But the CARE with which "nothing to see here, folks" has been worded in this article is... well... something to see.

Mind you, in a country where we oppose literacy tests for voters, we should probably oppose numeracy tests as well.

So a few (or, reportedly, about 1/3) of US voters who read "0.009 percent" don't understand either the concept of percent or the function of a decimal point.

But it would be hypocritical to resort to the increasingly popular "they shouldn't be voting anyway." There's no "good disenfranchisement." 

All I ever asked for (but rarely got) was reportage with enough epistemological humility to admit that errors are at least possible.

We now have one company's AI hacking "accidentally" into another company's AI. Machine errors do exist.

A postbox containing mail-in ballots could be hit by a truck or submerged in a flood.

And yes, an occasional poll worker at an under-staffed polling place (rural or urban) may think "that there candidate don't need these here votes" and glance about to see if anyone is watching.

Of course all of this is IMPOSSIBLE. Until it happens. Then the spin is... something to see.

Let's admit that occasionally a referee misses a call, but that's part of the game, as we've seen recently. 

Failure to admit fallibility comes off as gaslighting, and sometimes that generates more rage than the offense about which you're being gaslit.

So this isn't the cheap car beating the expensive one, the Vistiq costs more to buy. But it's the more expensive vehicle that ends up saving me money, because of what happens after you drive it home. The Tahoe gets 17 mpg. At current gas prices that's about $5,880 a year in fuel. The Vistiq gets 2.7 miles per kWh, and I charge it at home almost every time. Its yearly "fuel" bill is about $1,111. That's a gap of nearly $4,800 a year, for the same miles driven.

Every IT organization understands the concept of "technical debt". This is a naturally occurring phenomena of IT, every advance will require some remediation of earlier code and will, or may, broaden the aperture in which that tech can be applied. Adjustments will need to be made. This is understood by everyone in tech.

Open AI's "effort" to try and avoid the consequences of its tech is plain. If the US still had a Congress, they'd be passing laws to ensure that the effects of AI on its downstream victims, er, users, is fully paid for by the AI companies and not by taxpayers - either directly or indirectly.

That Open AI may be "working with" their present victim ought to be no indication of future action or future responsibility. Building a legal structure that more clearly lays out the obligations of these AI companies is the job of Congress, and, well, us.  Electing people willing and able to stand up for AI's future victims, er users, is critical to ensuring AI works for us and not the other way around.

Slapping a massive fine on OpenAI for "negligence" would be a start.

Further, the accounting department would ask the contractor's receiving institution to provide their wire instructions (or ACH) for transmission of the funds. There should be several safeguards in place that would catch this. 

Finally, their IT Dept. is way behind the times. In larger cities, they're known to send out phishing test emails to staff to determine who might need additional training. If you got caught clicking on something, you would get an email of shame, along with training.

Ross Douthat’s recurring panic about declining birthrates always presents itself as civilizational concern, but the pattern is unmistakable: he, along with figures like Elon Musk and J.D. Vance, frames population decline as an existential threat specifically to Western, white, Euro‑American civilization. His demographic alarmism isn’t neutral; it’s cultural self‑preservation dressed up as policy analysis.
Douthat insists he’s diagnosing a universal human problem, yet the anxiety he returns to, again and again, is the shrinking share of people who look like him. He rarely acknowledges that population decline is not inherently catastrophic, nor that many societies thrive with stable or modestly shrinking populations. Instead, he treats fertility as a moral duty owed to his own cultural lineage, implying that the world is endangered if white Americans and Europeans don’t produce more children.
This is why he gets it wrong. His argument isn’t about humanity; it’s about heritage, economic sustainability and cultural continuity. And by masking cultural panic as demographic science, he avoids confronting the obvious: the real threat to liberal democracy isn’t fewer babies, it’s the refusal to imagine a future not centered on one dominant culture.
Douthat critiques populists for magical thinking, but his own demographic obsession is its own form of elite mythmaking: a story in which “civilization” collapses unless one particular civilization reproduces itself indefinitely.

comments.body: Mr. Greggs opening line, "American recently learned . . . " is one of the most dishonest statements ever printed in the WSJ.  The challenges with America's Social Security system have been well known for decades.  The correct opening line should read, "America's largest retirement program is and has long been in shambles.  The primary reason for that reality is the failure of wisdom and will by America's political leaders."  Older Americans are currently and quickly being pushed toward a catastrophic financial cliff that will crush many.  And the hands on that wheel chair have not been those of the Republican members of Congress alone.

comments.name: Alan Lewis
comments.body:
The SS Trust Funds hold about $2.5 trillion, mandated to be 100% Treasury securities. Long-term, it would likely prove a better idea to allow these funds to be more diversified: say 40% stocks + 60% bonds (Treasuries + Corporates). This could be administered as "total market" index funds at very low rates. I suggest Vanguard.

As the Trust Funds are being depleted to zero, this is not a complete solution. But it is a blueprint for "new" Trust Funds, which need to be funded.

Re funding, a major problem is demographics. It would be very helpful for the US to develop a long-run population growth target of, let's say, 2% growth per year on average. Adjust immigration flows (and urban planning) accordingly.

In principle, there should be bi-partisan appeal. It's a good project for the 2026-2028 Congress, which probably isn't going to get much done anyway. The Republicans get "entitlement reform". The Democrats get "immigration reform". Go for it.

I recommend thinking about how much the federal government is spending on three ostensively unrelated but major undertakings: trying to reduce the global HIV/AIDS epidemic; waging war against Iran: and implementing “immigration enforcement.” 
In April, the State Department announced that, by cutting US  contributions to PREPFAR by 30 percent in 2026, the Trump Administration has saved the lives of many of the 24 million human beings infected with HIV/AIDS. It stated:
"In the coming months... the narrative will shift as our strategic approach demonstrates that ending the HIV/AIDS epidemic requires fewer taxpayer dollars—not more."
But how can you have a health initiative that is both “America First” and “Global”? And how can you spend less money and still presume to “end” a global epidemic that has killed 43.2 million people. With the 30% reduction, the US will contribute about $6 billion dollars. 
By comparison, the war against Iran has so far cost $37.5 billion. Moreover, on July 21, the Times reported that “Mr. Hegseth and the Trump administration are requesting as much as $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the war.” 
Finally, the projected federal budget for “immigration enforcement” in 2026 is approximately $30 billion.

Perhaps the Trump administration and its Congressional allies can figure out how to achieve more when it comes to two violent undertakings—the war and immigration enforcement—by spending less of taxpayers’ money.

Add to this list John Ford's "The Wings of Eagles," about early naval aviator, and later screenwriter, Frank "Spig" Wead. Ford and Wead worked on pictures together, including "They Were Expendable."

Ostensibly a biopic, Ford lets the cat out of the bag in a story session with Wead and director "John Dodge," where a book titled "Ulysses" is on the conference table. While Ford dodges the reference with a comic line so inane that many may see the link as accidental, the film's convergence of plot points affirms a connection. A key scene has Wead succumb to the song of a siren: his young daughter's late night cry that sets him tumbling in a ruinous fall.

Dan Dailey, a onetime navy buddy to John Wayne's Wead, is a Eumaeus on steroids, a Zelig presence with a godlike ability to appear whenever crises, conflicts, and conundrum's cross Wead's path. 

Maureen O'Hara is the Penelope here, keeping the home fires burning and having to pick up the pieces of her husband's peripatetic careers. Strictures on her existence are captured metaphorically in a series of shots, as she removes and replaces clothes on a line. An open yard leading to the sea, a brilliant sky with clouds aloft, clothing bouncing on the line, her hair and dress fretted in a breeze--all are visual phrases that Ford assembles into a poem on the strain of an existence locked into that of another, when a horizon of opportunity beckons.

Ford's adaptive take on The Odyssey is centered on passion and well worth a view.

What struck me about this article is that it is all about what Autistic people can do to make their travel bearable, and nothing about what other people could do to support us. What about asking for a little understanding and accommodation from non-autistic (I won’t say “neurotypical” becuase no one is typical!) people?

In the excellent book “Unmasking Autism”, Devon Price makes a point that I hadn’t really understood before: as an autistic person, I’m disabled. I had a hard time accepting this, because there are so many people who have far more difficult situations than I do. What I learned is that it isn’t about being unable to do something, but not being able to do it because the majority of people have built the world around assumptions that don’t apply. So, someone in a wheelchair can’t use the bathroom because they have been *dis*abled by a design that doesn’t provide a large door and handrails.

Here are some things that non-autistic people can do to not disable people like me:

1. Allow us to move and vocalize in ways that might not feel “normal”. I can’t tell you how much harm it does to have to constantly suppress my need to flap my arms or how helpful it can be to be able to wander aimlessly in circles. But if I did that in an airport, someone would call security.

2. Be mindful of noise from electronics, bright lights, strong smells and aggressive movements.

3. Listen to people when they tell you that something is hard or they don’t know what to do.

An important point needs to be made, particularly given some of the comments I have seen in this string.

Rare diseases collectively affect more than 300 million people worldwide, yet the knowledge required to understand and treat them remains fragmented across thousands of publications, specialist insights, and emerging discoveries. Although each rare disease affects relatively few patients individually, there are approximately 6,000–8,000 identified rare diseases.

So when viewed on a "siloed", high specific basis as these conditions must, it can look to be a poor use of health funding, that might buy cheaper solutions for more - but it does not work that way.  The solutions for one rare disease, inevitably carry over to others, and across disciplines.  One might think that only a few hundred are being helped, but it  more likely over the years will be millions.

A metaphor - technology you take for granted in your car today started in F1 racing - it's like that.

comments.name: Jaganathan
comments.body:
Articles like this reveal a persistent, human-centric bias: we routinely confuse technological output with the broader definition of intelligence.
We celebrate when monkeys recognize geometric shapes or crows use basic tools, viewing these as primitive steps toward "human-like" smarts. Yet, we completely ignore the profound, complex intelligence already operating across the natural world. An eagle intercepting a moving rabbit mid-flight is executing real-time predictive physics and dynamic mathematics that would baffle a supercomputer. A parasitic queen ant executing a hostile takeover of a rival colony by chemically hacking the workers' communication lines is pulling off a strategic feat rivaling any corporate coup.
Our "superior" intelligence allowed us to build an environment of engineered abundance, flattening the natural dopamine rewards of scarcity and discovery that our brains evolved to thrive on. In disconnecting ourselves from nature to exploit it, we created a world our ancient biology struggles to find peace in—and then mistakenly assume that because other animals didn't build rockets to Mars, they lack intelligence.
Perhaps it’s time to stop measuring animal intelligence by how closely it mirrors our own, and start appreciating how flawlessly they execute their own complex math, chemistry, and systemic balance within the world they belong to.

Without Wagner, Bayreuth would be just another provincial town in central Europe; to those who are wnthralled by this great music, the trip is well worth the effort. Yes, the theater can be unbearably hot and humid; yes, the restaurant scene isn' that of a major city. comments.name: Ed Christian
comments.body: I earned a Ph.D. in English lit. in 1983 because I loved reading fiction and poetry and wanted to help students learn to love them and figure them out. I liked the New Critics (who had been new decades before). Only a one grad students mentioned “Theory”. A few years after I started my professorial career, suddenly it became difficult to get any articles or books accepted for publication that weren’t mostly about “Theory.”  I read the people mentioned in this review and realized the proponents were much smarter than me and seemed uninterested in what I loved. Theory was mostly a way to separate the elite intellectuals from the rest of us and make it almost impossible for us to publish. In 34 years as a professor, only one colleague who studied under Derrida was actually interested in theory or wrote about it, and he got fired for playing around. Philosophy should be kept away from literary criticism, and literary criticism should help books come alive for students.

comments.name: Felix
comments.body:
I arrived as a grad student in a literature department, at one of the hotspots, in the heyday of “theory” (80s). A few things struck me at the time and strike me even more now. 

The first is that you were implicitly expected to have already read the stuff before you began grad school. At the time, significant undergraduate exposure to “theory” was a hallmark of an education at one of the Ivies, along with a few other elite institutions and the odd school into which some young professor happened to have imported it. Otherwise, not so much.

To make matters worse, you couldn’t make up for the deficiency in your education by way of course work. French post-structuralists permeated the discussion in the classroom but were never on the syllabus. So you had to be reading it, in addition to the material actually on the syllabi, in your spare time. As well as curating the look, of course. It was "a lot."

The other thing that struck me was that most of the material was philosophy, not literary criticism. I wanted to discuss novels and soon discovered that most people had very little interest in novels. What they wanted to talk about was “theory.” Cool for them but boring for me.

Unlike some of my not-previously-initiated peers, I did not develop a chip on my shoulder about “theory.” I actually enjoyed it, up to a point. I just couldn’t fathom why people allowed it to dominate as it did and why students of literature found philosophy so much more compelling than literature.

The department had a list of alums, so I looked at it to see where they’d wound up (would I get a job?). A number had indeed become philosophy profs, but those from the 60s and 70s had all written about . . . existentialists. A shelf load of books about Sartre never to be read again. At that moment I realized philosophy wasn’t immune to fads and fashions, and did something else with my life. Almost 40 years on, it seems to me Foucault had something to say. The rest, eh.

He was going with a group led by a philosophical friend and mentor I did know very well, Michel Serres. They decided to go to a restaurant I didn’t like, so I joined up with another group. I warned Derrida that the only reason Serres (usually a very trustworthy guide) was recommending the restaurant they were going to was that he liked to order the chimichanga – not that he liked the chimichanga – he only liked saying “chimichanga.”

The weather has become more unpredictable and devastating for humans and nature alike. Hot weather has extended time frames now. Scientists have found that summer temperatures start earlier and last longer which adds about 6 extra days of hot temps every decade. 

Still, there are those who turn a blind eye to climate change which by now  is really a climate crisis. Effective measures to at least halt more devastation to the environment seem largely unpopular, are only implemented half-heartedly only to be revoked when political leadership changes.

Some old favorites, especially in Southeast Asia.   

Some new and creative choices here in the states: I've not seen Bentonville AR, but know the state to have lots of hidden beauty.

My only quibble would be Big Sur.  It's not a good choice any longer, and I too love the road and views.  

The crowding and excessive prices make this a destination best skipped for most, especially during the summer, when traffic jams turn the journey into a slow crawl behind large RVs.

I strongly suggest looking for less overrun choices if you wish to include a Californian road trip, an excellent idea.

Route 395 along the east side of the Sierras remains uncrowded, and although there are known sights like Mount Whitney (the trailhead portal store is worth the drive up to the cool heights where the hikes start), there are plenty lesser known places to see as well.

There are petroglyphs the BLM will offer a map for at Bishop, many mountain roads to escape the valley heat, hot springs, both wild and developed, horseback riding among waterfalls (Red's Meadow).  

Whoa Nellie remains one of the more unexpected dining opportunities, a cafe at a gas station on the turn off to Yosemite.  The food has been delicious for decades and the prices are a third of what Big Sur restaurants charge.  Same for Tom's, down the road.  

The Lost Coast remains obscure and easily visited for those looking for a beach trip, and Point Reyes also offers many choices: even Marin is more affordable than Big Sur.

There are some missing nuances, whether from the book or the review, maybe because of space limitations.
Commenters picked up that it matters what realm of life we’re talking about; inherent rights or talent or accomplishment?

Those in the anti-equality camp can sill contribute to equality. Think of Carnegie and the funding of libraries. What enhances the prospects of equality more than that?
Intellectualism does not have to come at the expense of compassion. I assume some tech bro’s see their work as enhancing equality.

At three thousand meters in open air with peaks all around us the fear was at first exhilarating, then stifling. And then, paralyzing. comments.name: Tony Adams
comments.body: I was a journalist on a ten day white water rafting/camping trip in the Grand Canyon. On the first full day, without any warning, our guide led us up the canyon wall to the ancient granaries. The heights were more extreme than those in the Ausable Chasm, and there is no safety cord. At one point I froze. Then one leg started shaking, and there was the cold sweat,  and I felt like I might pass out. I was working through that as those behind me passed me on the narrow path while I clung to the rock side of the canyon. Far below us was the river and our distant raft that looked tiny. I handed one of my fellow travelers my camera as he passed me and asked him to take my photo, as no one would ever believe I had done this. I now look at that picture and at the fear in my face and relive it entirely. I finally got the courage to rejoin the group at the dizzying destination, mostly because I didn't want to be the guy who couldn't do it. The rest of the trip was easier for me. I've been on that trip about a dozen times, now as a host.

I do wonder why young people were drawn to Charlie Kirk. To give one example, Kirk was a climate change denier and young people will be disproportionately affected by climate change impacts.

Charlie Kirk spoke on climate change frequently, framing environmentalism as a political weapon meant to expand government control and undermine capitalism. His core arguments centered on four themes:

Denying the Existential Threat: He disputed the scientific consensus on human-caused global warming, calling the idea of a climate crisis "gibberish" and "balderdash."

Climate as "Marxism": He argued that climate activism was a Trojan horse for economic redistribution, famously stating, "Climate change is the wrapper around Marxism."

Fossil Fuel Advocacy: He actively promoted hydrocarbons, arguing their cheap, reliable energy was essential for economic growth and lifting people out of poverty.

Opposition to Green Policy: He fiercely opposed the Green New Deal, the Paris Climate Accord, and renewable subsidies, claiming they crippled U.S. industry and drove up energy costs for working families.

The only thing that I can think of is that we have a big problem with science education in this country, in particular climate science.

comments.name: Brandon Budovlya
comments.body: investigation found that Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle have $1.65 trillion in debt that doesn't appear on their balance sheets, more than the $1.35 trillion they officially report. These are GPU contracts, data center leases, and joint ventures that don't count as debt under accounting rules until the facilities go live. Meta's hidden debt is $420 billion, triple its reported debt. Oracle's grew 30-fold in four years. All five declined to comment. My Take Nikkei examined the actual filings and put a number on something the BIS already flagged as "shadow borrowing" back in March. These companies owe more off their balance sheets than on them, and the accounting rules let them keep it that way until the data centers go live. That's legal, but it means investors looking at quarterly earnings this week are seeing less than half the picture. Four of these five report earnings in the next two weeks. The reported debt will look manageable. The $1.65 trillion in footnotes won't make the headlines. But when those data centers start operating, the leases hit the books all at once. If AI demand comes in below projections, those facilities get marked down and the losses land on the investors and insurance policyholders who funded the construction through private credit and project bonds without realizing how much total exposure they were carrying.
